impossible.capability: Programmatic removal of the OS Bluetooth bond (removeBond via reflection, both drivers)
impossible.why: iOS provides no public or private API to remove a Bluetooth pairing from the app. Bond removal is exclusively a user action in Settings → Bluetooth → ⓘ → Forget This Device. This is not a missing convenience: three of the Tandem driver's safety-relevant recovery paths (status 0x05 before connect, status 0x08 with no prior session, three consecutive zero-response connections) and both drivers' unpair paths call removeBond, and a stale bond is exactly what blocks a successful re-pair. Android's hidden-API reflection has no analogue — and private-API use would additionally be caught by App Store Connect's static analysis on TestFlight upload, breaking the fork-and-build distribution model.
impossible.closest_alternative: Detect the condition and hand the user an explicit, non-dismissible guided remediation: a sheet stating the pump no longer trusts this phone, with numbered steps for Settings → Bluetooth → ⓘ → Forget This Device and an Open Settings button, then a Retry Pairing action that verifies recovery. `CBError.peerRemovedPairingInformation` makes the most important case reliably detectable — better than Android's status-byte guessing. Preserve the load-bearing counter-rule in the new form: never show the forget-device instruction when `hadSuccessfulSession` is true, because transient encryption renegotiation across sleep/wake resolves itself and a needless forget forces a physical re-pair.

impossible.why: Android calls `refresh()` by reflection on every connect specifically to prevent a stale cached characteristic table from silently dropping notifications — a failure mode that presents as a connected pump delivering no data. iOS caches discovered services and characteristics per bonded peripheral and exposes no way to flush that cache. The only invalidation paths are the peripheral sending a GATT Service Changed indication or the user forgetting the device.
impossible.closest_alternative: Handle `peripheral(_:didModifyServices:)` and re-run discovery for the invalidated services, and re-discover services on every fresh connection rather than caching handles in app memory. Then detect the symptom rather than pre-empt it: reuse the existing MAX_ZERO_RESPONSE_CONNECTIONS = 3 heuristic — reaching `.connected` three times with zero notifications received — and route it to the guided Forget This Device flow above. This turns an invisible silent-data-loss failure into an actionable one, which is arguably better than Android's fail-soft `refresh()` that logs a WARN and continues.

impossible.capability: Medtronic advertising payload parity (manufacturer data 0x01F9, TX-power inclusion, advertise-interval mode)
impossible.why: `CBPeripheralManager.startAdvertising(_:)` accepts exactly two keys: `CBAdvertisementDataLocalNameKey` and `CBAdvertisementDataServiceUUIDsKey`. Manufacturer-specific data cannot be advertised from iOS at all. The Android implementation deliberately carries the "Mobile NNNNNN" name as manufacturer data (0x00 + ASCII name + 0x00) under company id 0x01F9 with `setIncludeDeviceName(false)`, mirroring the proven JavaPumpConnector advertisement that the pump's matcher was reverse-engineered against. iOS also gives no control over advertising interval (the BALANCED-for-first-pair vs LOW_LATENCY-for-reconnect distinction, which exists because the paired pump scans infrequently) and no control over TX-power inclusion.
impossible.closest_alternative: Advertise the SAKE service UUID (0xFE82 first-pair / 0xFE81 reconnect) plus the name via `CBAdvertisementDataLocalNameKey`, which iOS emits as the standard GAP Complete Local Name AD type, and validate on real hardware whether the pump's `Mobile .{0,7}` matcher reads the GAP local name or only the manufacturer-data copy. If it reads only manufacturer data, Medtronic pairing cannot be implemented on iOS by any means available to a third-party app. This is unverifiable without a physical MiniMed pump, which neither the lead developer nor the maintainer has.

impossible.capability: Background BLE advertising visible to a non-Apple peripheral (Medtronic RECONNECT-mode indefinite wait)
impossible.why: Apple documents that when an app advertising via CBPeripheralManager moves to the background, the local name is removed from the advertisement entirely and all service UUIDs are relocated to a special 'overflow' area that can only be discovered by another iOS device explicitly scanning for those exact UUIDs. A Medtronic pump is not an iOS device and cannot read the overflow area. Medtronic's entire reconnection model is 'advertise in RECONNECT mode indefinitely because the pump scans infrequently' — which requires the phone to be discoverable for hours while the user is not looking at their phone. That is precisely the condition iOS makes impossible.
impossible.closest_alternative: Foreground-only Medtronic pairing and foreground-only Medtronic reconnection: the user must open the app and keep the pairing screen on screen for the pump to find the phone. An already-established Medtronic link does survive backgrounding (the `bluetooth-peripheral` background mode keeps GATT-server reads, writes, and notifications alive), so the degradation is specifically at re-establishment after any drop. There is no workaround. This makes the documented Medtronic promise "Once paired, the pump is remembered — GlycemicGPT reconnects on its own" false on iOS, and the docs and in-app copy must say so.

impossible.capability: Foreground service (PumpConnectionService) as an execution construct
impossible.why: iOS has no foreground services, no `startForeground`, no `START_STICKY`, no service restart semantics, and no user-visible ongoing notification that guarantees process survival. There is no object corresponding to PumpConnectionService, so its documented decision — start the service only once the connection state enters {CONNECTING, AUTHENTICATING, CONNECTED} to avoid `ForegroundServiceDidNotStartInTime` when a phone cannot advertise — describes a problem that does not exist on iOS.
impossible.closest_alternative: The `bluetooth-central` and `bluetooth-peripheral` UIBackgroundModes plus CBCentralManager/CBPeripheralManager state preservation and restoration (`CBCentralManagerOptionRestoreIdentifierKey`) give the actual capability the service existed to provide: an indefinite BLE link maintained in the background, with the app relaunched into the background on connect, disconnect, scan match, or characteristic notification, and `willRestoreState` called before the manager reports its state. Restoration resumes Core Bluetooth work only — it cannot resume arbitrary background processing, so any non-BLE work the service did (backend sync, polling scheduling) must be re-established from within the CB delegate callbacks or scheduled via BGTaskScheduler. Keep the state-based trigger point as the moment to start a Live Activity and register background work.

impossible.capability: Wake locks and battery-threshold wake-lock policy (PARTIAL_WAKE_LOCK, 20 min timeout, 15 min renewal, 2 min reconnect lock, release below 5%)
impossible.why: iOS exposes no wake-lock API of any kind. `UIApplication.isIdleTimerDisabled` only prevents screen dimming in the foreground and does nothing for background CPU. There is no way to hold the AP awake, no `setReferenceCounted`, no renewal loop, and no way to trade battery for reliability. The entire policy — including the safety-relevant coupling where releasing the lock below 5% battery can silently stop 15 s keep-alive polling against a pump that drops idle links at ~30 s — has no iOS surface to express.
impossible.closest_alternative: Rely on Core Bluetooth background mode, which keeps a connected link alive without any app-held resource and wakes the app on incoming notifications — removing the need for a wake lock for the connection itself. What is genuinely lost is app-scheduled periodic work while backgrounded: iOS will not reliably run a 15 s timer in the background. Restructure keep-alive to be pump-driven (subscribe to a characteristic the pump notifies on) rather than phone-timer-driven wherever the protocol allows, and use BGAppRefreshTask only as an opportunistic watchdog, never as the mechanism data flow depends on. Retain `ProcessInfo.isLowPowerModeEnabled` and `UIDevice.batteryLevel` as inputs to polling cadence, dropping the wake-lock release thresholds entirely.

impossible.capability: Permanently visible ongoing notification carrying the alert-floor honesty text
impossible.why: The Android foreground-service notification is unconditional, permanent, silent, low-importance, undismissable, and always present while the service runs — and it is the only backgrounded surface stating whether anything is watching for lows and highs, with `lastFloorStatus` caching existing specifically so a redundant service start cannot overwrite "Alerts degraded — this phone is NOT watching for lows or highs" with reassuring copy. iOS has no undismissable persistent notification. Live Activities, the closest construct, are user-dismissable, end after roughly 8 hours of active display, and are removed from the Lock Screen after roughly 12 hours; a standard UNNotification is dismissable and does not persist.
impossible.closest_alternative: A three-part substitute that preserves the safety property without claiming permanence: (1) a Live Activity on the Lock Screen and Dynamic Island showing pump connection state and alert-floor status while paired, restarted whenever the app runs and its `staleDate` passes; (2) an unconditional in-app status banner on Home carrying the same three floor strings, which is not time-limited; (3) a repeating local notification at `.timeSensitive` interruption level whenever the floor status is FloorNotWatching, so a degraded state cannot go silently unobserved after the Live Activity expires. Whatever is built must never state or imply that alerts are active when the floor status is unknown or degraded — port the pessimistic-seed and cache-don't-overwrite rules to the new surfaces verbatim.

impossible.capability: Guaranteed app relaunch after user termination (START_STICKY + RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED equivalence)
impossible.why: Android's service is START_STICKY and BootCompletedReceiver restarts it after reboot whenever a pump is paired. On iOS, CB state restoration does relaunch the app into the background after a device reboot once the user unlocks and a matching Bluetooth event occurs — so the reboot case is covered. What is not covered: if the user force-quits the app from the App Switcher, iOS deliberately suppresses all Core Bluetooth relaunch for that app until the user manually opens it again. No entitlement, background mode, or API changes this.
impossible.closest_alternative: Configure CBCentralManager and CBPeripheralManager with restore identifiers so reboot and system-eviction relaunch work, and implement `willRestoreState` to re-adopt restored peripherals and re-arm the pending connection. For force-quit there is no technical mitigation — the only honest response is disclosure: a prominent, permanent statement in Settings, in onboarding, and in the docs that swiping the app away in the App Switcher stops background pump monitoring, plus a detection heuristic (long gap since last successful background wake) that surfaces a Time Sensitive notification the next time the app does run.

ios_requirements: The app must let a user reach a dedicated pairing flow from Settings via a pump card that shows current pairing status, offering Pair Pump when unpaired and Re-pair when paired, and must return the user to Settings automatically once the pump reaches the connected state.

The pairing flow presented must be determined by the active pump driver, supporting both a phone-scans-and-user-enters-a-code flow and a phone-is-discoverable-and-waits flow, and must change live when the user selects a different driver in Settings.

All pairing screen copy, blurbs, and code-entry instructions must be supplied by the active driver rather than hard-coded to one vendor, so a driver is never described with another vendor's instructions.

The app must expose a single connection state with the seven states disconnected, scanning, connecting, authenticating, authFailed, connected, and reconnecting, consumed identically by the pairing flow, the home status row, the debug view, the polling gate, and the read gateway.

During a scan the user must see nearby pumps identified by name and detected model with a live-updating signal strength, ordered strongest-first, with devices removed from the list when they stop advertising, and must be able to stop the scan at any time.
A scan must stop automatically after a bounded period of no user interaction so the radio is not left running indefinitely when the user leaves the pairing screen open.

When a scan cannot start, the user must be told which specific condition prevents it — Bluetooth turned off, Bluetooth permission denied, or Bluetooth unavailable on this device — rather than the scan silently ending.

The user must be able to enter a pairing code of 6 to 16 characters with no character-class restriction, no truncation below 16, and no auto-correction or auto-capitalisation, and must be able to edit and resubmit that code after a rejection without re-selecting the pump.

The user must be told, before the system Bluetooth prompt appears, why the app needs Bluetooth, and if permission is denied must be given a one-tap route into the app's iOS Settings pane, with the denial state clearing automatically when they return with permission granted.

While the app is connecting or authenticating the user must be able to cancel and return to the previous step, and the app must surface a retry path if the attempt has not resolved within a bounded time.

When pairing is rejected, the user must be shown which category of failure occurred — wrong or expired code, pump no longer trusts this phone, secure handshake timed out, pump already paired to another phone, or Bluetooth unavailable — not a single generic failure message.

When the pump has removed its pairing information for this phone, the app must present step-by-step instructions to forget the device in iOS Settings and then retry pairing, and must verify recovery afterwards.

The app must never present the forget-device instruction, or treat a disconnection as a trust failure, when a successful authenticated session has previously been established with that pump and the user has not unpaired.
Once paired, the app must attempt to reconnect to the pump indefinitely, with no attempt limit and no give-up condition, until the user explicitly unpairs.

The app must maintain and re-establish the pump connection while backgrounded and while the device is locked, and must resume that connection automatically after the app is evicted by the system or after the device reboots and is unlocked.

The app must clearly and permanently inform the user that force-quitting the app from the App Switcher stops background pump monitoring until the app is opened again, and must notify the user if a prolonged gap in background activity is detected.

The user must be able to see current pump connection status from outside the app while paired, on the Lock Screen and Dynamic Island, including whether the phone is currently watching for lows and highs.

When the app is not watching for lows and highs, that degraded state must be communicated on a surface that does not expire, and the app must never display reassuring alert-status copy when the true status is degraded or unknown.

For a driver that requires the phone to be discoverable to the pump, the flow must tell the user that the app must remain open and on screen while waiting, and must state that reconnection after a drop also requires reopening the app.

The user must be warned before pairing that a pump connects to only one phone at a time and that the pump must be removed from the manufacturer's official app first, on both the pairing screen and the Settings pump card.

Unpairing must have one behaviour regardless of where it is initiated: cancel the connection, stop any advertising, erase that driver's stored credentials, end any external status display, and then instruct the user to complete removal in iOS Settings.
Unpairing must require an explicit confirmation before it takes effect.
Pairing credentials must be readable by the app while the device is locked so overnight reconnection works, must not leave the device, and must not be restored onto a different device.
Credentials for one pump driver must be isolated from every other driver, so selecting a different driver never overwrites or exposes another driver's pairing.
The app must never display a raw device identifier as the user-facing name of a paired pump; it must identify the pump by name and model.
A failed reconnection or authentication that occurs while the user is not on the pairing screen must be surfaced to the user rather than being silently absorbed.
The connection status shown on the home screen must be tappable when pairing has failed, taking the user directly to the pairing flow.

The app must present a background-monitoring health check in Settings covering notification authorization, Bluetooth authorization, Low Power Mode, Background App Refresh, and force-quit status, with a route to resolve each.
A maintainer must be able to exercise every pairing state, every failure mode, and the full reconnection lifecycle in the iOS Simulator through a simulated pump driver, without Bluetooth hardware.
A maintainer must be able to capture a real pairing and reconnection session on physical hardware and replay it as an automated regression test.
The watch app must expose no pairing, scanning, code entry, or unpairing capability, and must display forwarded pump connection status only.

The app must state in-product and in documentation which pump drivers are validated against physical hardware on iOS and which are unvalidated, and must not present an unvalidated driver as production-ready.

risks.risk: Medtronic advertise-and-wait pairing may be entirely unimplementable on iOS. The pump's advertiser matcher was reverse-engineered against an advertisement carrying the 'Mobile NNNNNN' name in manufacturer data under company 0x01F9, and iOS cannot advertise manufacturer data at all. If the pump does not also accept the GAP Complete Local Name that iOS emits, there is no workaround available to a third-party app, and the parity goal of 'every supported device' cannot be met.
risks.mitigation: Treat this as a spike that must run before any Medtronic iOS work is scheduled: build a minimal CBPeripheralManager advertising the 0xFE82 service plus a local name and test against a physical MiniMed pump. Neither the lead developer nor Daniel has one, so sourcing hardware or a community tester is a prerequisite. Sequence Tandem first and gate Medtronic on the spike result.

risks.risk: Even if Medtronic first-pair works, Medtronic reconnection after any disconnect requires the app to be in the foreground with the screen on, because iOS strips the local name and hides service UUIDs in an iOS-only overflow area when advertising in the background. The shipped promise that the pump reconnects on its own is false on iOS, and a Medtronic user loses monitoring silently whenever the app is not open.
risks.mitigation: If Medtronic ships on iOS at all, it must ship with explicit in-app and documented disclosure of foreground-only reconnection, a persistent reconnect-needed notification when a paired Medtronic pump has been disconnected past a threshold, and a clear statement that the driver is not suitable as a sole monitoring path.

risks.risk: Bond removal is impossible on iOS, so all three Tandem trust-failure recovery paths become manual user procedures. A user who does not follow the Settings → Forget This Device instruction is left permanently unable to re-pair, with no data and a screen that keeps saying pairing failed.
risks.mitigation: Make the remediation flow blocking and instrumented: detect `CBError.peerRemovedPairingInformation` and the three-zero-response condition, present numbered steps with an Open Settings deep link, and verify recovery by attempting a fresh connection afterwards. Add a Time Sensitive notification if the condition persists past a threshold so the user is not waiting on a screen they never open.

risks.risk: Porting the Tandem two-phase backoff literally onto iOS would replace a strictly better native primitive (an indefinite, kernel-serviced pending connection that costs the app nothing and survives termination) with connect/cancel churn that drains battery and can miss reconnection windows while the app is suspended.
risks.mitigation: Explicitly specify the pending-connect model in the architecture and add a code-review rule forbidding attempt caps, give-up conditions, and app-scheduled reconnect timers in the connection layer. Preserve the counters for diagnostics only, exactly as Android does with consecutiveReconnectFailures.

risks.risk: The alert-floor honesty text loses its permanence guarantee. Live Activities are user-dismissable and expire after roughly 8 hours active and 12 hours on the Lock Screen, so a degraded 'NOT watching for lows or highs' state can silently disappear from every out-of-app surface overnight — the exact window the app exists to cover.
risks.mitigation: Do not rely on the Live Activity alone. Pair it with a non-expiring in-app banner and a repeating Time Sensitive local notification whenever the floor status is degraded, and port the pessimistic-seed and never-overwrite-an-honest-degraded-status rules to every new surface.

risks.risk: Critical Alerts entitlement is effectively unobtainable under the fork-and-build distribution model. `com.apple.developer.usernotifications.critical-alerts` requires per-Team-ID approval from Apple, and every user builds under their own Apple Developer account. A pairing or connection failure therefore cannot break through Focus or a silenced ringer.
risks.mitigation: Design for `.timeSensitive` interruption level, which requires only an entitlement any developer can enable with no approval, and document plainly that alerts respect Do Not Disturb and the ringer switch. Do not build any flow that assumes critical alerts are available.

risks.risk: The entire subsystem is unverifiable by the lead developer. Core Bluetooth is absent from the Simulator, he has no iPhone and no Apple Watch, and the single hardware validator has a Tandem pump only. Regressions in pairing, reconnection, and bond-loss handling could ship undetected.
risks.mitigation: Make the BLE seam a first-class architectural requirement: a transport protocol with a scriptable fake driver that can produce every connection state and every fault in the Simulator, plus record/replay of real hardware sessions as regression fixtures. Treat any code path only reachable through real CB objects as needing an explicit hardware sign-off checklist item.

risks.risk: Choosing the wrong Keychain accessibility class silently breaks overnight reconnection. `kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlocked` would make pairing credentials unreadable while the device is locked, so background reconnects would fail in exactly the scenario that matters most, and would fail quietly rather than visibly.
risks.mitigation: Mandate `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly` for all pairing credentials, add a unit test asserting the attribute on every stored item, and add a hardware test step that locks the device, disconnects the pump, and verifies reconnection while locked.

risks.risk: The MAC-to-CBPeripheral.identifier substitution can fail to round-trip. The identifier is not stable across app reinstalls or across devices, and can change for a peripheral that is not yet bonded, which would present as a pump that was paired yesterday being unfindable today.
risks.mitigation: Store a composite identity (CB identifier plus last advertised local name plus last-seen time) and, when `retrievePeripherals(withIdentifiers:)` returns nothing, fall back to a service-filtered scan that matches the stored name and re-binds the identity silently. Cover this with an explicit reinstall-and-recover test on hardware.

risks.risk: Force-quit permanently disables Core Bluetooth relaunch for the app until it is manually reopened. Users routinely swipe apps away, and this failure mode is invisible: the app simply stops monitoring with no notification, no badge, and no system indication.
risks.mitigation: Disclose it prominently in onboarding, Settings, and the docs; record the last successful background wake and surface a Time Sensitive catch-up notification when the app next runs after an anomalous gap; keep the Live Activity present while paired so its disappearance is itself a visible signal.

risks.risk: TestFlight builds expire after 90 days, so under the fork-and-build model every user must re-run the pipeline quarterly or the monitoring app stops launching. Pairing state survives, but the app does not.
risks.mitigation: Warn in-app starting roughly two weeks before build expiry with the exact rebuild steps, and document the expiry cadence alongside the pairing instructions so users do not discover it during a monitoring gap. Consider a scheduled GitHub Actions workflow in the fork template that rebuilds and uploads automatically.

risks.risk: The lost ability to request MTU 185 and high connection priority means the Tandem link runs at whatever parameters iOS negotiates. If the negotiated MTU is smaller than the protocol's packetisation assumes, or the connection interval is longer than the pump's idle timeout tolerates, symptoms will look like protocol bugs rather than link-configuration issues.
risks.mitigation: Read `maximumWriteValueLength(for:)` after connection and assert it meets the protocol minimum, failing loudly with a diagnostic rather than proceeding. Log negotiated link parameters in the debug view so a hardware validator can report them, and confirm keep-alive cadence against the pump's roughly 30-second idle-link drop on real hardware.

risks.risk: The two divergent Android unpair paths, if ported as-is, are worse on iOS: the weaker Settings path would leave an orphaned pending connection registered with the OS, a Live Activity running, and a bond that the app can never remove, while the user believes the pump is disconnected.
risks.mitigation: Specify one canonical unpair operation invoked from both entry points, with confirmation and the Forget This Device follow-through, and add a test asserting that after unpair there is no pending connection, no advertising, no stored credentials, and no active Live Activity.

questions_for_pm: Given that Medtronic advertise-and-wait pairing on iOS cannot reproduce the manufacturer-data advertisement the pump's matcher was reverse-engineered against, and that even in the best case iOS makes background re-advertising invisible to the pump — meaning Medtronic reconnection would require the user to open the app and keep it on screen — does iOS ship Medtronic at all? The options are: (a) ship it as an explicitly foreground-only, manually-reconnected BETA driver with prominent disclosure, accepting that it is not a safe sole monitoring path; (b) hold Medtronic off iOS until the GAP-local-name spike passes on physical hardware, and ship Tandem-only in the interim; or (c) drop Medtronic from iOS permanently and state that device parity with Android is not achievable on this platform. This is a scope and patient-safety-communication decision that cannot be resolved from the Android repo or from Apple's platform rules.
